newsitem.title: GERMANY: Pace of more German tax cuts unclear -official.
newsitem.headline: Pace of more German tax cuts unclear -official.

text.p: The pace of further German tax cuts remains unclear at the weekend, two days after the centre-right coalition government agreed to several key reductions in 1998.

Ending months of feuding, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition of Democrats (CDU) and Free Democrats (FDP) last week pledged to cut two points off the so-called solidarity tax to finance German unification, lowering it to 5.5 percent in 1998.
But at the weekend Wolfgang Schaeuble, the powerful CDU parliamentary leader, told German newspaper Bild am Sonntag the pace of future cuts in the unpopular tax was still undecided.
"We cannot continue to cut the solidarity tax at that pace, even though we had once thought this would be possible."
Last week's deal would lead to a 30 billion mark reduction in taxes, Schaueble said, adding, "Then we cannot consider taking another step to reduce the solidarity tax again."
The cut in the solidarity tax and a reduction of corporate taxes would take effect on January 1, 1998 and the cuts would be financed by commensurate reductions in state spending.
Although Schaueble said the tax would be eliminated at some point, "no one can say when that will be."

Separately German finance minister Theo Waigel told German paper Welt am Sonntag that the tax reform would jump-start consumer demand and revive investments, leading to an immediate 0.5 percentage point rise in economic growth.

To finance the tax reform the coalition also said it plans a new tax on energy consumption which would result in a sharp rise in the value added tax and needs to be approved by the European Commission.
FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle told German newspaper Express, "There are clear signs from Brussels that such a tax could be approved."
Separately he told the newspaper that his party wanted to focus more on pension reform.
